title: American Revolution
sentences: The American Revolution (1765–1789) was a political movement in the Thirteen Colonies of Great Britain.

It began as a colonial rebellion and evolved into a revolution, the result of which was the creation of the United States following the colonies' victory in the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) and British recognition of their sovereign independence in the Treaty of Paris.
The Second Continental Congress, as the provisional government, established the Continental Army and appointed George Washington as its commander-in-chief in 1775.
In May 1776, Congress voted to suppress all forms of Crown authority, to be replaced by locally created authority, and each state created a constitution.
The Congress passed the Lee Resolution for independence on July 2 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4 arguing for the separation based on "inalienable rights".
The individual member states together created a shared sovereignty under the Articles of Confederation to facilitate international affairs and the promulgation of the war.

Throughout most of the conflict the outcome appeared uncertain, but a decisive 1781 victory by combined French and Continental Army forces commanded by Washington in the Siege of Yorktown led King George III and the Fox–North coalition in government to negotiate the cessation of British colonial rule, and the acknowledgment of American sovereignty.
A more centralized federal republic was created with the passage of the Constitution of the United States that took effect in 1789, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
Discontent with British colonial rule began shortly after the end of the French and Indian War in 1763.

Although the Thirteen Colonies had fought and supported the war directly, the British Parliament imposed new taxes on the colonists, ostensibly to compensate for wartime costs, and transferred control of the colonies' western lands to British officials in Montreal.

In 1765, Representatives from several colonies held the Stamp Act Congress in New York City, resulting in the Declaration of Rights and Grievances, which argued that taxation without representation, among other British policies, violated their rights as Englishmen.
The Stamp Act was repealed in 1767, but tensions increased again following Parliament's passage of the Townshend Acts.
In an effort to quell the mounting rebellion, King George III deployed British troops to the colony of Massachusetts, which resulted in the Boston Massacre in 1770.
In December 1773, a local faction of the Sons of Liberty orchestrated the Boston Tea Party, during which they dumped chests of taxed tea owned by the British East India Company into Boston Harbor.
Parliament responded by enacting a series of punitive laws, called the Intolerable Acts.
These were intended to end self-government in Massachusetts, but instead increased American support for revolution.
In 1774, twelve of the Thirteen Colonies sent delegates to the First Continental Congress (the Province of Georgia joined in 1775) in order to begin coordinating Patriot resistance.
In August 1775, King George III proclaimed Massachusetts to be in rebellion.
The British subsequently attempted to disarm the colonists, resulting in the Battles of Lexington and Concord and starting the Revolutionary War.
The Second Continental Congress convened in May 1775 and created the Continental Army, which soon laid siege to Boston and forced the British to withdraw by sea in March 1776.
On July 2, the Congress passed the Lee Resolution, affirming their support for joint independence.
On July 4, 1776, they unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence.
The Revolutionary War continued for another seven years, with France and Spain eventually entering.

On September 28, 1781, Washington commanded the Continental Army's capture of a British army under General Cornwallis at the Siege of Yorktown, leading to the collapse of King George's control of Parliament.
Consensus in Parliament soon shifted to the war ending on American terms.

On September 3, 1783, the British signed the Treaty of Paris, recognizing the sovereign independence of the United States, and ceding to the new nation nearly all the territory east of the Mississippi River and south of the Great Lakes.

The United States became the first nation to establish a federal republic with a written constitution based on the principles of universal natural rights, consent of the governed, and equality under the law, although with significant democratic limitations compared to later evolution of the concept.
After the Glorious Revolution in England, the British had adopted a strict trade policy of "salutary neglect," whereby the Thirteen Colonies were largely left to govern themselves.

The British political establishment, especially after taking massive swathes of land from the former territories of New France, pursued a policy of greater control over colonial affairs, prompting the Thirteen Colonies to seek restoration of greater autonomy from Britain.
The Thirteen Colonies were established in the 17th century originally as part of the English Empire and later as part of the British Empire after the union of England and Scotland in 1707.
The development of a unique American identity can be traced back to the English Civil War (1642–1651) and its aftermath.
In that period the Puritan colonies of New England supported the Commonwealth government responsible for the execution of King Charles I.
After the Stuart Restoration of 1660, Massachusetts did not recognize Charles II as the legitimate king for more than a year after his coronation.

In King Philip's War (1675–1678), the New England colonies fought a coalition of a few American Indian tribes without military assistance from England, thereby contributing to the development of a uniquely American identity separate from that of the British identity.
In the 1680s, Charles and his brother, James II, attempted to bring New England under direct English control.
The colonists fiercely opposed this, and the Crown nullified their colonial charters in response.
In 1686, James finalized these efforts by consolidating the separate New England colonies along with New York and New Jersey into the Dominion of New England.
Edmund Andros was appointed royal governor and tasked with governing the new Dominion under his direct rule.
Colonial assemblies and town meetings were restricted, new local taxes were levied, and rights were abridged.
Dominion rule triggered bitter resentment throughout New England.
When James tried to rule without Parliament, the English aristocracy removed him from power in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.
This was followed by the 1689 Boston revolt, which overthrew Dominion rule.
Colonial governments reasserted their control after the revolt.
The new monarchs, William and Mary, granted new charters to the individual New England colonies.
After the Glorious Revolution, the British Empire became a constitutional monarchy with sovereignty in the King-in-Parliament.
